title: Why Meetings Are Often Less Productive Than They Could Be
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues meetings underperform because they demand real-time thinking about unfamiliar material, which is cognitively hostile to depth. Because most attendees arrive without having wrestled with the issue beforehand, discussions stay shallow and lack energy or genuine debate. The remedy is deliberate prework -- pre-reads, data review, option analysis, or scenario response -- that moves the heavy thinking outside the meeting so the room can focus on debate and decisions. The author closes with a provocation: if an issue isn't worth asking people to prepare for, it may not be worth a meeting at all.
points: Meetings ask people to form opinions on the fly, which the author calls cognitively hostile to deep thinking.
Amazon's practice of a silent six-page pre-read before discussion illustrates one model for shifting thinking outside the room.
Prework -- pre-reads, data review, anonymous surveys, scenario response -- surfaces disagreement and sharpens the questions people bring.
If a topic doesn't justify asking people to prepare, the author suggests that's a signal the meeting itself may not be necessary.
quotes: They must form an opinion while digesting facts, data, and other people’s opinions. The overload makes critical and sound thinking all but impossible.

Without having thought through relevant points, tested their viewpoints against what they already know, and searched for mental models and analogies that offer insight, people are caught off guard and stay at the surface level of inquiry.
Not every organization has to go as far as Amazon, which asks team members to silently read a six-page decision brief before the discussion begins, but the point is worth highlighting.
The real goal of prework is to move heavy thinking out of the meeting so the discussion can make significant progress.
If a meeting isn’t worth doing the upfront preparation for a more intense discussion, then maybe the leader should ask whether the meeting is necessary at all.
